results.title: Nebius Raises AI GPU Cloud Prices as Compute Demand Surges
highlights:
Nebius is raising pay-as-you-go prices for selected NVIDIA GPU cloud instances as demand for artificial intelligence computing continues to strain available capacity.

Beginning October 1, selected NVIDIA GPU rates will increase roughly 17% to 21%, according to Reuters. Some CPU-only instances will rise about 25%, while selected memory offerings will increase about 41%. The move marks Nebius’ second price increase in three months.

The increases provide another signal that the AI infrastructure boom is extending beyond GPUs. Large AI clusters also require substantial power, cooling, networking, CPUs and memory, putting pressure across the physical data-center stack.

Nebius said customers reserving large-scale clusters for multiple months can receive commitment discounts. Reuters also reported that the company’s recent AI cloud growth included four customer contracts averaging more than $1 billion each.

results.title: Adam Sioud | Modelling GPU rental prices
highlights:
For this article, there is a good example to look at in May 2026. RTX 3090 asking prices on Vast.ai rose sharply, then fell back in June. And there was a dataset on Hugging Face with data on these listings. So I wanted to explore it. I don’t know exactly what drove the move, but there is data to work with. How can I wrangle it and play with it to get a clearer picture of what happened?

...

In mid-May, prices begin to leave that range. On May 30, the index reaches 240.1, while the baseline is 105.4: 128% above its baseline.

The main period above the range runs from May 14 to June 13, 31 days, using three consecutive days outside the band to identify a sustained change. Prices then fall back towards the baseline.

...

On May 30, 39 of 40 sellers were more than 10% above their April prices. Raising the threshold to 100% still leaves 34 of 40. For most of these sellers, prices had more than doubled.

The price rise lasted several weeks and involved most of the sellers that were tracked. Prices increased on individual listings, so cheaper offers disappearing cannot explain the rise on its own. Each search returns at most 64 listings, so this describes the sellers in the sample, but should still be indicative of the wider price movement.

...

Miners were renting GPUs to earn Pearl’s PRL token during the price rise. Tom’s Hardware reported on May 31 that miners were using RTX 4090 and 5090 instances on Vast.ai and RunPod, while a June study also reported people earning PRL on rented RTX 3090s. Alongside these reports, network hash rate shows the increase in mining activity, which is a big tell that mining PRL was directly linked to renting listings on Vast.ai.

So in a situation where PRL earnings can cover the rental cost and fees, miners have a reason to rent available listings, creating a strong incentive and big demand for the GPUs listed. As more listings are rented, buyers are left competing for less available capacity. In turn, that gives sellers an incentive to raise their asking prices. I think it’s clear that this demand from Pearl miners very likely contributed to the broad repricing in May. And while this was a sharper surge, we now also see more sustained demand affecting overall prices since the summer. So this is not a one-off event, in my opinion, and needs to be understood and studied more.

In addition, other GPU rental prices were rising too. AIMC’s report for May 25–31 recorded average on-demand prices up 4.9% for H100 SXM and 8.8% for H200 SXM. Very interesting.

results.title: What if you wake up tomorrow and the B300s you need are already rented out? | Sandeep Narahari
highlights:
B300 pricing is already moving around quite a bit. As of September 26, one GPU price tracker showed a $7.25/hour median across four providers, with listings ranging from $6.00 to $13.13/hour.

Another tracker recorded individual provider price moves of +46.6% and +89.1% within days in September. Those are provider-level moves, not a claim that the entire B300 market moved by that amount — but they show how quickly the market can change.

Availability can be just as unpredictable.

On September 11, GPU Finder reported only one provider with confirmed single-B300 capacity, even though other providers had listings that were out of capacity.

...

A 20% increase sounds small until you multiply it across a cluster.
At $7.25/GPU-hour, 32 B300s running 24/7 for 30 days costs about $167,040.
At 20% higher pricing, that becomes about $200,448.

That’s $33,408 more for one month.

Maybe prices go up 20%.
Maybe they don’t.

The point isn’t to predict the price.

results.title: Best GPU Cloud Providers for AI Startups in 2026: Real H100 and B200 Prices - Startupik
highlights:
The best GPU cloud for most AI startups in 2026 is a self-serve neocloud, not a hyperscaler. RunPod ($3.49 per H100 hour) and Lambda ($3.99) are the cheapest verified on-demand options for a single H100. Modal wins for bursty, serverless inference. Together AI wins when you can commit for 3 to 6 months. CoreWeave, AWS and Google only make sense once you need full 8-GPU nodes or already hold their credits.

One date matters right now. Nebius raises its on-demand prices on 1 October 2026, and most “cheapest GPU” lists have not caught up.

...

## Quick Verdict: Which GPU Cloud Should a Startup Pick?

- Cheapest single H100: RunPod Secure Cloud H100 SXM at $3.49 per hour, billed by the second, per RunPod’s pricing page.
- Price change to plan for: Nebius H100 goes from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour on 1 October 2026, and B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, per Nebius’s price page.
- Cheapest verified B200: Modal at $6.25 per hour of GPU time, followed by Lambda at $6.69.
- Best commitment discount with a public rate card: Together AI H100 falls from $3.99 on demand to $3.19 on a 91–180 day reservation.
- Minimum-unit trap: CoreWeave sells H100 only as an 8-GPU node at $49.24 per hour, which is $35,945 for a month of 24/7 use.
- Biggest free credits: Google for Startups offers up to $350,000 for AI startups, but only $250,000 of it lands in year one.

...

Second, prices are moving up at the self-serve end. Nebius, which offers no-commitment self-service up to 32 GPUs, lifts its on-demand rate card by 17% to 21% on 1 October. Any article or spreadsheet quoting $3.85 per H100 hour will be wrong within days.

...

### 3. Nebius: Strong Today, Repriced on 1 October

Why it works: Nebius offers self-serve access up to 32 GPUs with “no waitlists or minimum commitments”, after a $25 top-up. It publishes preemptible prices from $0.79 for H100 and H200 and from $0.99 for B200 and B300, the lowest spot entry points in this list.

When it breaks: The new rate card takes effect on 1 October 2026:

- H100: $3.85 to $4.50 (+17%)
- H200: $4.50 to $5.40 (+20%)
- B200: $7.15 to $8.50 (+19%)
- B300: $7.85 to $9.50 (+21%)

After the change, Nebius H100 is more expensive than Lambda, Together and RunPod on demand. Nebius is also the only provider here with a published egress fee: $0.015 per GiB for Standard object storage. Its startup credits are “currently available exclusively through” partner VC funds, for companies with $5M+ raised.

Use it if your workloads tolerate preemption, or you will negotiate a multi-month reservation (Nebius says up to 35% below on-demand). Skip it as your default on-demand provider after 1 October.

### 4. Modal: Best for Bursty Serverless Inference

Why it works: Modal bills GPU time per second: $0.001097 per second for H100 ($3.95 per hour), $0.001261 for H200 and $0.001736 for B200 ($6.25 per hour). You pay nothing while no request is running. The Starter plan is $0 per month with $30 of free compute each month.

When it breaks: The headline GPU price is not the full price, and every competitor list we read shows only the $3.95.

...

### 5. Together AI: Best Published Commitment Discounts

Why it works: Together publishes the full commitment ladder, which almost nobody else does. H100 is $3.99 on demand, $3.69 for 7–30 days, $3.45 for 31–90 days and $3.19 for 91–180 days. Preemptible H100 is $1.99. B200 runs from $8.19 on demand to $6.79 on a 91–180 day term.

When it breaks: Clusters start at a single 8-GPU node, so the entry ticket is eight GPUs, not one. Shared filesystem storage is $0.16 per GiB-month, roughly double Nebius or CoreWeave. Its older Instant Clusters launch blog quotes H100 at $2.20–$2.99, which conflicts with today’s pricing page; use the pricing page.

...

## What Does a Month of GPU Compute Actually Cost?

Rate cards are hard to compare in isolation. Here are two common startup workloads priced from the official pages above. Scenario A is one H100 serving inference 24/7 for 730 hours. Scenario B is a 72-hour fine-tuning run on 8 H100s (576 GPU-hours).

| Provider | A: 1x H100, 730 h | B: 8x H100, 72 h | What you are forced to rent |

| RunPod | $2,548 | $2,010 | 1 GPU |
| Nebius (until 30 Sep) | $2,811 | $2,218 | 1 GPU |

| CoreWeave | $35,945 (full node) | $3,545 | 8 GPUs |
| Google Cloud A3 High | $64,598 (full VM) | $6,371 | 8 GPUs |

Three things stand out. For the fine-tuning run, the spread between cheapest and most expensive is about 3x. For the always-on single GPU, it is about 25x, because the node-based clouds force you to rent seven idle GPUs.

Second, the Nebius change adds $475 per month to Scenario A. On a B200 it adds about $986 per month per GPU.

Third, preemptible capacity changes the fine-tuning math completely, if your training loop checkpoints often. The same 576 GPU-hours cost $1,146 on Together’s $1.99 preemptible H100 and from $455 on Nebius’s “from $0.79” rate. CoreWeave’s H100 spot node ($19.71 per hour) brings Scenario B to $1,419.

...

- Idle storage: RunPod doubles volume-disk price when a pod is stopped. Vast.ai’s docs say “storage charges continue even when instances are stopped”.
- Checkpoint storage: 2 TiB of shared filesystem costs about $143 per month on CoreWeave ($0.07/GB), $164 on Nebius ($0.08/GiB) and $328 on Together ($0.16/GiB).
- CPU and RAM on serverless: Modal adds both on top of the GPU line, plus region and non-preemptible multipliers.
- Upfront payment: AWS Capacity Blocks are paid when booked, which hits cash flow before the job starts.
- Egress: Free on Lambda, CoreWeave, Crusoe and RunPod. Nebius charges $0.015 per GiB on Standard object storage. On hyperscalers, egress beyond the free tier is a real line item.
- Balance cut-offs: Prepaid platforms like RunPod stop pods at a $0 balance. Set auto top-up before anything customer-facing runs there.
